**Neutralization removes the component of a signal that lies in the span of chosen factor exposures.** If a model's score is mostly high for large companies, it may appear predictive because it is taking a size exposure rather than finding independent information. Regressing the score on size and other selected factors separates that linear component. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html)

Let F contain exposure columns and a contain scores for the same cross-section. The weighted least-squares fit is F times beta, and the residual is $a_\perp=a-F\hat\beta$. The normal equations give $F^TW a_\perp=0$: the residual is orthogonal to the included exposures under the selected weighting.

**A small example.** If scores equal twice a sector indicator plus a residual, projecting onto that sector column removes the common sector component. Adding an intercept can remove the cross-sectional mean as well. QR or SVD provides a stable way to perform the projection when exposures are correlated; explicit inverses can be fragile.

Neutralizing scores does not automatically make a portfolio neutral. Position sizing, constraints, and later transformations can reintroduce exposure. Nor does linear orthogonality remove nonlinear or future risk. Evaluate whether the removed component was unwanted risk or useful signal, and validate the resulting portfolio separately under time-respecting assumptions.

**Technical details and references.**

Let $F$ contain cross-sectional factor exposures and $a$ the raw alpha vector. Regress alpha on exposures and keep the residual, using an intercept and weights where appropriate. [1](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/linear_model.html)

$$\hat\beta=(F^TWF)^{-1}F^TWa,\qquad a_\perp=a-F\hat\beta,\qquad F^TWa_\perp=0.$$

Use QR/SVD for numerical stability; Gram–Schmidt expresses the same projection idea with an orthonormal basis. This removes linear exposure to the included factors under the chosen weighting, not every nonlinear or future risk. Rank deficiency, changing exposures, constraints, and transaction costs matter.

Neutralizing predictions is different from constructing a factor-neutral portfolio: portfolio weights and risk estimates must also satisfy exposure constraints. Validate whether the removed component was unwanted risk or legitimate predictive signal.
